title: Living ashtpadi 20
hook: refuge is a place you can return to
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 21, salok: when there was nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy asked for, and your line: mercy, not reward. Did you give someone a little more mercy than they'd earned? Today we carry the whole twentieth ashtpadi out of the book. Day five hundred seventeen.

There's an old man in a lot of neighborhoods who has a bench. Same bench, same park, every morning, coffee in a paper cup. Nobody owns a park bench, but everyone knows it's his. And if you asked him why he comes, he probably wouldn't say anything grand. He'd say: it's where I sit. A refuge doesn't have to be a fortress. Sometimes it's just a place you keep coming back to, until coming back is part of who you are. That's how the twentieth ashtpadi gets lived.
screen: `THE SAME BENCH EVERY MORNING.` → `IT'S WHERE I SIT.` → `A PLACE YOU COME BACK TO.`

segments.voice: Here's the twentieth ashtpadi in brief. A traveler, after long wandering, phirat phirat, comes to God's saran, God's refuge, and falls there. Standing at the door, the traveler becomes a beggar, asking for the Name and the dust of good people's feet, and asking it as mercy, not reward. Saran is the key word. It means shelter, sanctuary, protection. In Sukhmani it's God's saran, a refuge that's God's to give. And in Sikh practice it isn't somewhere you reach once and never leave. The traveler came after wandering, and minds wander again. So refuge is something you return to. Daily. That's partly what the daily banis are for. Sikh practice sets aside the early hours, amrit vela, the ambrosial time before dawn, for sitting with the Name, and closes the day with Sohila. The days between can be loud; the refuge is there at both ends. Gurdwaras carry the same idea in stone. The Darbar Sahib in Amritsar has doors on all four sides, which Sikhs explain as open to anyone, from any direction. Gurdwaras keep a langar for whoever comes, and travelers find a meal there, and often a place to rest. And it doesn't have to be a building. For one person it's a corner of a bedroom with a small shelf. For another, a walk at dawn. The place matters less than the returning.
screen: `THE ASHTPADI: ARRIVE, ASK, RECEIVE.` · `SARAN: SHELTER THAT IS GOD'S TO GIVE.` · `RETURNED TO DAILY, AT BOTH ENDS.` · `DOORS ON FOUR SIDES.` · then, large: `REFUGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your quiet place. Look around the space you're in, or picture your home. Where could you sit for two minutes and not be interrupted? A chair by a window, the edge of a bed, a step outside. Go there now if you can, or picture it closely. Settle in. Breathe slowly. Let this become the spot you come back to. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru here. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 20. Saran, God's refuge, isn't reached once and left; Sikh practice returns to it daily, morning and night.
Your line: refuge. Today, come back to your quiet place one more time before you sleep, even for three breaths. Day five hundred seventeen.

screen: `DAY 517 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 21, SALOK: WHEN THERE WAS NOTHING.`

howItsDone: Sikh practice returns to God's refuge daily, sitting with the Name at amrit vela before dawn and reciting Sohila at night, and gurdwaras keep their doors and kitchens open to all.

pairs: the bani at the end of the day

myth: in Sikh practice, refuge is reached once and never left
the mind wanders again, so refuge is returned to, daily.
the Darbar Sahib in Amritsar has doors on all four sides
open to anyone, from any direction.
a refuge has to be a holy building
for some it's a corner shelf or a walk at dawn; the returning matters most.

fork.setup: you've found refuge once, on a good morning. by the twentieth ashtpadi, what comes next?
options: you're done; refuge is a one-time arrival.
come back to it, morning and night.
fork.reveal: Sikh practice returns to the refuge daily: amrit vela at one end, Sohila at the other.

original.note: Gurmukhi: saran, refuge or sanctuary; the salok's form is sarnaai.

trapdoor: what you thought: a refuge is where you hide when things go wrong.
what it means: a place, inner or outer, that you return to every day, which is God's to give.
what a scholar hears: the salok's own phrase is pariaa tau sarnaai, fallen at Your refuge, the devotee's posture in this ashtpadi.
